The reed is of cane and needs regular replacement. The pads are of leather or synthetic material, ensuring a good seal. An orchestral-key version was included in the patent, but few were made. From the early twentieth century until the Second World War it carried the bass line in jazz and dance bands; after the 1930s it declined because of its size, mechanical complexity and price, and the rise of the electric bass in the 1950s reduced demand further. Its lowest register has a full, dark quality with a strong resonance that produces impressive low-frequency vibration. Beside the warm brightness of the baritone saxophone the bass saxophone is fuller and steadier, close to the depth of the cello's and the horn's low register. Its resonance relies on the huge body, which effectively amplifies and strengthens the low-frequency waves, giving the sound both containment and penetration. In a band the bass saxophone often serves as a foundation colour, working with the bass of the brass to give a firm musical base. Its range is wide and expressive, able to convey quiet depth of feeling and also a commanding musical tension.

The bass saxophone is the fourth-lowest instrument in the saxophone family, lower in size and pitch than the common baritone saxophone; it has a present-day S-shaped body, and some models have a low A key. It is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 422.212-71, with Belgium as its regional marker. It is written in treble clef and sounds two octaves and a major second below the written note; the lowest written note is B-flat below middle C, sounding as A-flat1. It is not a commonly used instrument, but can be heard on 1920s jazz recordings, in free jazz, saxophone choirs and sextets, and is also occasionally used in wind bands and rock music.
